'''Herbert Leopold Strauss''' (March 26, 1936 &ndash; December 2, 2014) was an American chemist who specialized in [[spectroscopy]]. His family fled Nazi Germany and eventually immigrated to New York, where he graduated from Columbia University. He spent the entirety of his career at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

==Early life and education==
Herbert Leopold Strauss, who went by "Herb", was born on March 26, 1936, in [[Aachen]], Germany to parents Joan and Charles Strauss. He had a younger brother, Walter. The Strauss family escaped Germany in 1939, arriving in England.<ref name="Barnes"/><ref name="Ainsworth">{{cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i10/Herbert-L-Strauss.html| title=Herbert L. Strauss| website=C&EN| first=Susan J.| last=Ainsworth| date=March 9, 2015| access-date=10 November 2020}}</ref> While in London, Herbert Strauss was temporarily placed in an orphanage, where he became seriously ill from [[bronchitis]] and nearly died.<ref name="chronicle">{{cite news|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/sfgate/obituary.aspx?n=herbert-strauss&pid=173541012| title=Herbert Strauss| work=The San Francisco Chronicle| date=20 December 2014| access-date=10 November 2020}}</ref> The family eventually immigrated to [[Kew Gardens, Queens]] in New York City. There, his father worked as a real estate agent and his mother worked in a clothing store.<ref name="Barnes"/> Strauss received both a bachelor's degree (1957) and a PhD (1960) in chemistry from [[Columbia University]].<ref name="Ainsworth"/>

==Career==
Upon finishing his PhD, he spent a year conducting post-doctoral research at the [[University of Oxford]]. The first teaching position he accepted was at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]; he would remain at UC Berkeley for the rest of his career. He specialized in [[spectroscopy]], using [[Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy]] to determine the traits of various molecules. He also employed [[Raman spectroscopy]] and [[neutron spectroscopy]] "to study the rotations and vibrations of molecular hydrogen embedded in various systems".<ref name="Ainsworth"/>

From 1976 to 2000, he was the [[editor-in-chief|editor]] of the ''[[Annual Review of Physical Chemistry]]''.<ref name="chronicle"/> From 1995&ndash;2008, he was the Associate Dean of Undergraduate Affairs.<ref name="Barnes"/> He officially retired from Berkeley in 2003, though continued to teach until shortly before his death.<ref name="Ainsworth"/>

==Awards and honors==
In 1976, he was elected as a fellow to the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=S&year=2020&unit_id=&institution=| title=APS Fellow Archive| website=APS Physics| access-date=10 November 2020}}</ref> In 1994, he won both the Bomem-Michelson Prize for Spectroscopy and the [[Ellis R. Lippincott Award|Lippincott Award for Vibrational Spectroscopy]]. In 2003 he received the Berkeley Citation and Berkeley Faculty Service Award.<ref name="Barnes"/>

==Personal life and death==
In 1957, he met Carolyn North Cooper at a church in Manhattan during a midnight mass, despite both being Jewish.<ref name="Barnes"/> He and Carolyn had three children together.<ref name="chronicle"/> He enjoyed cycling, and commuted to and from campus each day via bicycle.<ref name="Barnes"/> Strauss died on December 2, 2014, at his home in [[Berkeley, California]], at the age of 78.<ref name="Barnes">{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/emeritus-chemistry-professor-herb-strauss-has-died-78| title=Emeritus chemistry professor Herb Strauss has died at 78| date=22 December 2014| first=Michael| last=Barnes| website=Berkeley College of Chemistry| access-date=10 November 2020}}</ref>
